title: The Magic Scroll: Leveraging biased noise to improve magic state cultivation in register-based architectures
authors: Ian D. Thorvaldson, Jeffrey Marshall, Jack R. Craig, Samuel K. Gorman, Charles D. Hill, Michelle Y. Simmons
abstract: Multiple quantum computing platforms across neutral atoms [1], nitrogen vacancy centres [2, 3], gate-defined dots [4-6] and 14|15 phosphorus atom qubits [7, 8] in silicon are experimentally exploring the use of high connectivity qubits, beyond that of nearest-neighbour planar lattices. Theoretical works consider modifications to fault-tolerant codes to leverage this higher qubit connectivity, such as non-local LDPC codes [9], inspiring superconducting [10] and photonic [11] platforms to also seek non-planar connectivity. In addition, separate theoretical works consider biased noise, where bit- and phase-flip errors are not equally likely. In this work, we present efficient methods for implementing 6.6.6 and 4.8.8 colour codes, as well as bilayer and folded surface codes, using two-qubit registers. We also leverage noise bias to avoid hook errors, demonstrating comparable performance to the surface code. By combining colour and bilayer codes, we show how magic state cultivation procedures [12-14] can be improved, in a procedure we refer to as the Magic Scroll. Not only does the Magic Scroll escape to a standard surface code, it also improves cultivation volumes by 3x and supports magic $|T\rangle$ state fidelities as low as $10^{-9}$. We show that this technique can be further leveraged to improve distillation performance, showing a 3x improvement to distillation volumes for error rates of $\sim 10^{-15}$. Through these constructions, we demonstrate techniques to leverage noise bias and high qubit connectivity, showing how register-based architectures can improve error rates and reduce quantum volumes in fault-tolerant quantum computing.
summary: This paper introduces the 'Magic Scroll,' a novel protocol for enhancing magic state generation in fault-tolerant quantum computing. It achieves this by combining color and bilayer error-correcting codes within multi-qubit register architectures that exploit intrinsic noise bias. The results demonstrate significant, quantifiable improvements (up to 3x) in both magic state cultivation and subsequent distillation volumes.
main_problem: The work aims to improve magic state cultivation and distillation procedures in fault-tolerant quantum computation by exploiting high qubit connectivity and intrinsic noise bias.
main_result: The proposed 'Magic Scroll' procedure, combining color and bilayer codes, improves magic state cultivation volumes by a factor of 3x and enhances distillation performance similarly.
method: The authors develop efficient implementations for various error-correcting codes (e.g., color codes, bilayer codes) using two-qubit registers and leverage noise bias to enhance these procedures.
model_or_system: The theoretical framework is built upon multi-qubit register architectures, applicable to platforms like silicon phosphorus qubits or neutral atoms. The analysis focuses on implementing surface and color codes under a biased error model where bit-flip and phase-flip errors are unequal.
key_observables: Magic |T> state fidelities (achieving $10^{-9}$), improvement factors for cultivation/distillation volumes ($\sim 3	imes$), and logical error rates ($\epsilon$).
important_parameters: Physical error rates ($p$) ranging from $0.05\%$ to $0.1\%$; the bias in noise (Z-errors); and code parameters like graph structures ($6.6.6$, $4.8.8$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumptions involve using multi-qubit registers for high connectivity, assuming a specific biased error model where idling errors are Z-biased, and employing empirical models for very large patch sizes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the physical qubit layout of register models, the 'Magic Scroll' procedure combining different codes, performance scaling comparisons between methods at varying physical error rates, and approximations for gapped code performance.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the architectural basis (multi-qubit registers), then detailing the implementation of advanced codes using noise bias, introducing the 'Magic Scroll' procedure to combine these elements, and finally performing detailed performance analysis on distillation volumes using complementary gaps for large patches.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete, mathematically derived protocols that directly address resource limitations (magic state availability) in fault-tolerant quantum computation by integrating hardware constraints (connectivity) with noise characteristics (bias).
